blogs.title: Section 1182(f) as Black Box: The Ninth Circuit Doubles Down on Trump v. Hawaii's Extreme Deference
blogs.description: This post analyzes the panel's conclusion that the President is likely to succeed on the merits of his authority under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) to suspend the entire U.S. Refugee Admissions Program. It examines how the panel applied Trump v. Hawaii's 'exudes deference' framework to foreclose any 'searching inquiry' into the President's justifications, and considers whether this reading effectively renders the Refugee Act of 1980—a statute that establishes an ongoing statutory framework for refugee admissions—a dead letter when the President invokes § 1182(f). The post also explores the doctrinal tension between § 1182(f)'s open-ended suspension power and Congress's detailed statutory scheme for refugee processing, and asks whether there are any textual limits on the President's authority that courts are willing to enforce post-Hawaii.

blogs.title: 'Shall' or 'May'? The Intra-Panel Split Over Whether Section 1522 Mandates Refugee Resettlement Funding
blogs.description: This post focuses on the sharp disagreement between the majority and Judge Lee's partial dissent over the interpretation of 8 U.S.C. § 1522. The majority reads the statute's use of 'shall' in § 1522(a) and specific subsections like (d)(2)(B) and (e)(7)(A) as imposing mandatory obligations on the executive to provide reception and placement services to admitted refugees. Judge Lee counters that the section's title ('Authorization for programs'), the repeated use of 'authorized' in the operative funding subsections (b)–(e), and the qualifying phrase 'In providing assistance under this section' all signal that § 1522 is permissive, not mandatory. The post analyzes the competing canons of construction, the role of statutory titles, the significance of 'to the extent of available appropriations' language, and the broader implications of this split for understanding when Congress mandates executive action versus merely authorizes it.

blogs.title: Terminated Contracts and Statutory Obligations: The APA Challenge That Survived the Stay
blogs.description: This post examines the panel's significant ruling that the government is likely to lose on at least one APA claim—specifically, the challenge to the State Department's termination of cooperative agreements with refugee resettlement organizations. It situates this holding within the broader legal landscape of executive agencies terminating contracts or funding arrangements that statutory schemes depend on, and considers the practical significance of the court's order directing the government to reinstate cooperative agreements necessary to provide § 1522 services. The post also analyzes the government's own representations about preparing new contract solicitations and the panel's apparent frustration with the executive's uncertainty about its capacity to meet statutory obligations, raising questions about whether an agency can evade statutory mandates by simply declining to maintain the contractual infrastructure needed to fulfill them.
